long_biography.plain_text:
Roy Nasser began programming early, first building a message-board network with childhood friend Albert Deweik and then a hosting business financed by his father’s first server. Their pre-Google search engine, Jarbas, nearly failed when the dot-com crash collapsed advertising prices. Rather than dismiss its support team, Nasser automated common enquiries; the prototype cut incoming email volume in half and revealed a product for other companies.

That insight became NeoAssist. Nasser drove its technical development as the founders spent years persuading businesses to adopt digital customer service, later repositioning the platform around omnichannel communications. A minority investment funded product and international expansion, and the company’s entire capital was acquired in 2021, with Nasser continuing as chief product officer. He subsequently moved into the family technology group, helping transform Compugraf into the cybersecurity-focused CG One.

uncertainties.detail: Roy Nasser is a moderately common name, but the Bina owner interview supplies a conclusive bundle of anchors: Brazilian nationality, exact 43-metre family yacht, 2013 acquisition, São Paulo base, software-company co-founder role, sister Sabina and father Jacques. Those details converge only on NeoAssist founder Roy Victor Nasser.

Oca Capital acquired all of NeoAssist in 2021, but the purchase price, Nasser's pre-sale percentage and his personal proceeds were not disclosed. The dossier therefore identifies enterprise software as the documented creation mechanism without estimating his personal fortune or attributing all family wealth to NeoAssist.

Endeavor explicitly records that Nasser's father founded a large technology business, paid for an early server and later invested with Albert Deweik's father in the Jarbas search engine. NeoAssist itself is documented as a separately created company, so Self-made — advantaged start fits better than inherited, mixed or independent-start classifications.

Nasser's current transformation-director role at CG One is well supported, and the company was founded by his father. Public sources reviewed do not establish Roy's present equity percentage or controlling authority, so the primary-industry field describes his operating role without treating him as the company's controlling owner.

The yacht interview says the family bought its first boat around 2001 when Nasser was seventeen, but that permits more than one birth year and does not establish a date or birthplace. Birth day, month, year and place therefore remain unproposed.

The owner interview identifies the family as Brazilian and Nasser as São Paulo-based, matching the upstream nationality and residence. It mentions mixed European and North African family backgrounds but does not establish a second nationality or stable secondary residence country.

Cybersecurity is Nasser's supported current operating field at CG One, but the reviewed evidence establishes only a relatively recent transformation-director mandate and does not show personal control or a separate wealth-creation mechanism. It remains in ordinary research context rather than receiving the approved Cybersecurity tag under the catalogue's stricter membership contract.

The LinkedIn profile is strongly identity-matched and CG One is a verified company website. No reliable personal website or Instagram account was found, and no Forbes social is proposed because the Forbes result is an article rather than a dedicated personal profile.

Bina is used only to resolve the upstream identity. Yacht acquisition, refit, charter and sale details are unrelated to Nasser's software wealth mechanism and are excluded from both biographies, classifications and tags.
